pamphlet_excerpts: Person-First Language: Many people with disabilities want to emphasize what they are able to do rather than emphasize their disabilities (p. 9).
Person-First Language Principle 2: Remember that people with disabilities are people first (p. 9).
Person-First Language Principle 3: Each person gets to decide how he or she should be described (p. 9).
Person-First Language Principle 4: You should use person-first language when talking about people who are not personal acquaintances or about people with disabilities as agroup (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Person-First Language): When you make a new friend or talk about an individual, show a person-first attitude by calling the individual what he orshe wants to be called (p. 9).
Step 2 (Person-First Language): Many people with disabilities see their condition as part ofwho they are, just like their gender, hair or eye color, or ethnicity (p. 9).
Step 3 (Person-First Language): Writing and talking with person-first language is a good habit to get into because it is the proper form for most situations (p. 9).
Step 4 (Person-First Language): Don't call someone an epileptic when you mean to say the person has epilepsy (p. 9).

Discuss what you have learned with your counselor.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Access. Visit TWO of the following locations and take notes about the accessibility to people with disabilities. In your notes, give examples of five things that could be done to improve upon the site and five things about the site that make it friendly to people with disabilities. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (1) Your school (2) Your place of worship (3) A Scouting event or campsite (4) A public exhibit or attraction (such as a theater, museum, or park) (b) Option B, Accommodation. Visit TWO of the following locations and take notes while observing features and methods that are used to accommodate people with invisible disabilities. While there, ask staff members to explain any accommodation features that may not be obvious. Note anything you think could be done to better accommodate people who have invisible disabilities. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (1) Your school (2) Your place of worship (3) A Scouting event or campsite (4) A public exhibit or attraction (such as a theater, museum, or park)

pamphlet_excerpts: Access / Accommodation: An accommodation is just a different way of doing things that is tailored to the individual needs of a person with a disability (p. 36).
Access / Accommodation Principle 2: Most schools are accommodating students with disabilities to make learning better (p. 36).
Access / Accommodation Principle 3: Accommodations also happen in workplaces to make work easier and in public attractions to make experiences more enjoyable (p. 36).
Access / Accommodation Principle 4: For requirement 4b, you are to identify accommodations that already exist at certain places and suggest better accommodations (p. 36).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Access / Accommodation): You will need to talk with staff members at the locations or facilities to help you understand the accommodations, because they often are not obvious (p. 36).
Step 2 (Access / Accommodation): Next time you are in a public place, look at how accessible (usable) the location is for people with disabilities (p. 36).
Step 3 (Access / Accommodation): Some of the accessibility projects suggested in this pamphlet might be done as service projects for achieving the ranks of Star, Life, or Eagle (p. 36).
Step 4 (Access / Accommodation): Ifyou wish to do aproject for rank advancement, check with your Scoutmaster to be sure your undertaking meets the standards for leadership service (p. 36).

Volunteer with a program or agency for eight hours. (c) Using resources such as disability advocacy agencies, government agencies, the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission), and news magazines, learn about myths and misconceptions that influence the general public's understanding of people with disabilities. List 10 myths and misconceptions about people with disabilities and learn the facts about each myth. Share your list with your counselor, then use it to make a presentation to a Cub Scout pack or other group.

Step 3 (Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination): Fact: Overall, people with disabilities live like anyone else (p. 19).
Step 4 (Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination): The attitude that a disability ruins a person's life can be more disabling than the disability itself (p. 19).
